## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Race Condition in Account Lockout Enforcement Enables Brute-Force Bypass
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:678-713`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:678-713
                // 5. Check Lockout Status
                if (user.isLocked()) {
                    if (user.getLockedUntil() != null && Instant.now().isAfter(user.getLockedUntil())) {
                        // Lockout period expired; automatically unlock
                        user.unlockAccount();
                        auditLogger.logAccountUnlocked(correlationId, trimmedUser, "Lockout duration expired");
                    } else {
                        PasswordSecurity.performDummyVerification(password);
                        auditLogger.logAttemptOnLockedAccount(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, user.getLockedUntil(), maxFailedAttempts);
                        return AuthenticationResult.locked(correlationId);
                    }
                }

                // 6. Verify Password (Constant-Time)
                boolean passwordValid = PasswordSecurity.verifyPassword(
                    password,
                    user.getSalt(),
                    user.getIterations(),
                    user.getPasswordHash()
                );

                // 7. Handle Result
                if (passwordValid) {
                    user.recordSuccess();
                    auditLogger.logSuccess(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, maxFailedAttempts);
                    return AuthenticationResult.success(user.getUsername(), user.getRole(), correlationId);
                } else {
                    int currentFailed = user.incrementFailedAttempts();
                    if (currentFailed >= maxFailedAttempts) {
                        user.lockAccount(lockoutDuration);
                        auditLogger.logAccountLocked(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, maxFailedAttempts, lockoutDuration);
                        return AuthenticationResult.locked(correlationId);
                    } else {
                        auditLogger.logBadPassword(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, currentFailed, maxFailedAttempts);
                        return AuthenticationResult.failure(correlationId);
                    }
                }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`AuthenticationService.authenticate()` is not synchronized, and the account lockout check (`user.isLocked()`) occurs prior to the computationally intensive password verification step (`PasswordSecurity.verifyPassword()`, which executes 100,000 PBKDF2 iterations taking ~50-100ms).

An attacker can transmit dozens or hundreds of concurrent login attempts in parallel for a targeted account. Because all parallel threads check `user.isLocked()` before any single request completes its PBKDF2 hash and increments `failedAttempts` at line 704, every concurrent thread passes the lockout check while `failedAttempts < maxFailedAttempts`. All threads proceed to verify their candidate passwords against the stored hash. This time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition allows attackers to bypass the 5-attempt brute-force restriction (CWE-307) and test large password batches without being locked out.

**Fix:**
Synchronize the lockout verification and attempt recording around the user account, or atomically track in-flight verification requests per user to ensure that no further verification occurs once the failure threshold or concurrency threshold is reached.
```java
                boolean passwordValid;
                int currentFailed = 0;
                boolean shouldLock = false;
                boolean isCurrentlyLocked = false;
                Instant lockedUntil = null;

                synchronized (user) {
                    if (user.isLocked()) {
                        if (user.getLockedUntil() != null && Instant.now().isAfter(user.getLockedUntil())) {
                            user.unlockAccount();
                            auditLogger.logAccountUnlocked(correlationId, trimmedUser, "Lockout duration expired");
                        } else {
                            isCurrentlyLocked = true;
                            lockedUntil = user.getLockedUntil();
                        }
                    }
                }

                if (isCurrentlyLocked) {
                    PasswordSecurity.performDummyVerification(password);
                    auditLogger.logAttemptOnLockedAccount(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, lockedUntil, maxFailedAttempts);
                    return AuthenticationResult.failure(correlationId);
                }

                passwordValid = PasswordSecurity.verifyPassword(
                    password,
                    user.getSalt(),
                    user.getIterations(),
                    user.getPasswordHash()
                );

                synchronized (user) {
                    if (passwordValid) {
                        if (user.isLocked()) {
                            auditLogger.logAttemptOnLockedAccount(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, user.getLockedUntil(), maxFailedAttempts);
                            return AuthenticationResult.failure(correlationId);
                        }
                        user.recordSuccess();
                    } else {
                        currentFailed = user.incrementFailedAttempts();
                        if (currentFailed >= maxFailedAttempts) {
                            user.lockAccount(lockoutDuration);
                            shouldLock = true;
                        }
                    }
                }

                if (passwordValid) {
                    auditLogger.logSuccess(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, maxFailedAttempts);
                    return AuthenticationResult.success(user.getUsername(), user.getRole(), correlationId);
                } else if (shouldLock) {
                    auditLogger.logAccountLocked(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, maxFailedAttempts, lockoutDuration);
                    return AuthenticationResult.failure(correlationId);
                } else {
                    auditLogger.logBadPassword(correlationId, trimmedUser, effectiveIp, currentFailed, maxFailedAttempts);
                    return AuthenticationResult.failure(correlationId);
                }
```

### SEC-02: Log Injection and Log Forging via Unsanitized `role` Parameter in Registration Audit Log
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-117: Improper Output Handling for Logs
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:520-532`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:520-532
        public void logUserRegistered(String correlationId, String username, String role, String clientIp) {
            AuditEvent event = new AuditEvent(
                correlationId,
                AuditEventType.USER_REGISTERED,
                sanitizeForLog(username),
                sanitizeForLog(clientIp),
                "SUCCESS",
                "ACCOUNT_PROVISIONED",
                0,
                0,
                "New user registered with role " + role
            );
            logEvent(Level.INFO, event);
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
While `username` and `clientIp` are processed through `sanitizeForLog()`, the `role` parameter is concatenated directly into the `details` field (`"New user registered with role " + role`). `registerUser()` (lines 610-627) accepts `role` directly from caller input without validation or character restrictions. Furthermore, `AuditEvent.toStructuredLogString()` embeds `details` directly into `details=\"%s\"` without performing any sanitization.

If a registration request supplies a `role` containing newline characters (`\r\n`), the newline is written directly to `authentication_audit.log` via the `FileHandler` custom formatter (`record.getMessage() + System.lineSeparator()`). This enables an attacker to inject arbitrary counterfeit audit log records (for example, forging fraudulent `AUTH_SUCCESS` events or attributing actions to administrators). Additionally, injecting unescaped quotation marks (`"`) breaks key-value pair parsing in SIEM log parsers.

**Fix:**
Sanitize `role` using `sanitizeForLog()`, validate `role` against an allowlist of valid roles, and sanitize `details` inside `AuditEvent.toStructuredLogString()` as a defensive boundary control.
```java
        public void logUserRegistered(String correlationId, String username, String role, String clientIp) {
            String safeRole = sanitizeForLog(role != null ? role : "USER");
            AuditEvent event = new AuditEvent(
                correlationId,
                AuditEventType.USER_REGISTERED,
                sanitizeForLog(username),
                sanitizeForLog(clientIp),
                "SUCCESS",
                "ACCOUNT_PROVISIONED",
                0,
                0,
                "New user registered with role " + safeRole
            );
            logEvent(Level.INFO, event);
        }
```

### SEC-03: User Enumeration via Observable Response Discrepancy on Account Lockout
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-204: Observable Response Discrepancy
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:564-567`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:564-567
        public static AuthenticationResult locked(String correlationId) {
            // Can be generic or slightly informative; generic prevents account enumeration
            return new AuthenticationResult(false, "Invalid username or password or account is locked", null, null, correlationId);
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
When an authentication attempt fails on an active account, `AuthenticationResult.failure()` returns the generic message `"Invalid username or password"`. However, when an account is locked (lines 686 and 708), `AuthenticationResult.locked()` returns `"Invalid username or password or account is locked"`.

For a non-existent username, `userOpt.isEmpty()` is always triggered (line 662), consistently returning `AuthenticationResult.failure()` regardless of how many failed attempts are submitted. For an existing username, submitting 5 consecutive invalid passwords triggers `user.lockAccount()`, changing the response message to `"Invalid username or password or account is locked"`. An external unauthenticated attacker can therefore enumerate valid usernames by submitting 5 incorrect passwords for target candidate usernames and observing whether the response message changes.

**Fix:**
Return the identical, uniform error message (`"Invalid username or password"`) across all authentication failure modes, including lockout. Keep the lockout distinction purely in internal audit logs.
```java
        public static AuthenticationResult locked(String correlationId) {
            // Return uniform error message to prevent user enumeration
            return new AuthenticationResult(false, "Invalid username or password", null, null, correlationId);
        }
```

---

### SEC-04: Exposure of Plaintext Password via CLI Arguments and Hardcoded Admin Credentials
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-214: Invocation of Process Using Visible Sensitive Information
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:762-771`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:762-771
            } else if ("--login".equalsIgnoreCase(args[0]) && args.length >= 3) {
                String username = args[1];
                String password = args[2];
                String ip = (args.length >= 4) ? args[3] : "127.0.0.1";
                // Register a default user if database is empty
                authService.registerUser("admin", "AdminSecret123!".toCharArray(), "ADMINISTRATOR", "127.0.0.1");
                AuthenticationResult result = authService.authenticate(username, password.toCharArray(), ip);
                System.out.println("Authentication Outcome: " + result);
                return;
            }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
1. **Plaintext CLI Argument Exposure (CWE-214)**: The `--login` CLI command reads the user password directly from `args[2]`. Command-line arguments are visible in the operating system's process table to all local users via `ps aux`, `top`, or `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, and are stored in shell history files (`.bash_history`).
2. **Hardcoded Credentials (CWE-798)**: Line 767 silently provisions a default administrative account with the hardcoded username `"admin"` and password `"AdminSecret123!"` whenever `--login` is executed. Hardcoded credentials embedded in source code can be extracted and abused by attackers to gain administrative access.

**Fix:**
Remove hardcoded administrative provisioning from the login handler. Prompt for passwords interactively using `System.console().readPassword()` without echoing characters or exposing them via process arguments.
```java
            } else if ("--login".equalsIgnoreCase(args[0]) && args.length >= 2) {
                String username = args[1];
                String ip = (args.length >= 3) ? args[2] : "127.0.0.1";
                char[] password;
                if (System.console() != null) {
                    password = System.console().readPassword("Enter password for %s: ", username);
                } else {
                    Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
                    System.out.printf("Enter password for %s: ", username);
                    password = scanner.nextLine().toCharArray();
                }
                AuthenticationResult result = authService.authenticate(username, password, ip);
                System.out.println("Authentication Outcome: " + result);
                return;
            }
```

### SEC-05: Insecure Default File Permissions and Unbounded Growth on Audit Log File
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:350-357`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:350-357
            // File audit trail output
            try {
                FileHandler fileHandler = new FileHandler(logFilePath, true);
                fileHandler.setLevel(Level.ALL);
                fileHandler.setFormatter(customFormatter);
                LOGGER.addHandler(fileHandler);
            } catch (IOException e) {
                System.err.println("Warning: Could not create audit log file: " + e.getMessage());
            }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
1. **Insecure Permissions (CWE-732 / CWE-276)**: `new FileHandler(logFilePath, true)` creates `authentication_audit.log` using the process default umask. On Linux systems, this results in world-readable permissions (`0644` / `rw-r--r--`). Audit logs contain sensitive operational security metadata—including valid usernames, client IP addresses, authentication attempt volumes, and lockout statuses—which are exposed to all local unprivileged users and container co-tenants.
2. **Unbounded Growth / Denial of Service (CWE-770 / CWE-400)**: Calling `FileHandler(logFilePath, true)` configures append mode without setting a maximum file size limit or log rotation count. During high traffic or credential-stuffing attacks, the log file will grow without bound until disk space is exhausted, causing system denial of service.

**Fix:**
Explicitly set restrictive POSIX permissions (`0600` - owner read/write only) upon file creation, and configure `FileHandler` with file size limits and rotation counts.
```java
            // File audit trail output with rotation and restricted permissions
            try {
                File logFile = new File(logFilePath);
                if (!logFile.exists()) {
                    boolean created = logFile.createNewFile();
                    if (created) {
                        logFile.setReadable(false, false);
                        logFile.setReadable(true, true);
                        logFile.setWritable(false, false);
                        logFile.setWritable(true, true);
                        logFile.setExecutable(false, false);
                    }
                }
                // Rotate logs at 10 MB with up to 5 archive files
                int limitBytes = 10 * 1024 * 1024;
                int fileCount = 5;
                FileHandler fileHandler = new FileHandler(logFilePath, limitBytes, fileCount, true);
                fileHandler.setLevel(Level.ALL);
                fileHandler.setFormatter(customFormatter);
                LOGGER.addHandler(fileHandler);
            } catch (IOException e) {
                System.err.println("Warning: Could not create audit log file: " + e.getMessage());
            }
```

---

### SEC-06: Missing Password Complexity and Minimum Length Enforcement in Registration
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-521: Weak Password Requirements
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:613-616`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:613-616
                if (username == null || username.trim().isEmpty() || password == null || password.length == 0) {
                    auditLogger.logInvalidInput(correlationId, username, clientIp, "Username or password cannot be empty during registration", maxFailedAttempts);
                    return false;
                }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`registerUser()` only verifies that `password` is non-null and `password.length > 0`. It does not enforce a minimum length (e.g. at least 12 characters per modern NIST/OWASP guidance), nor does it enforce character complexity or block easily guessable single-character passwords. Users can register passwords as short as 1 character (e.g. `"a"`), making accounts trivial to compromise through online guessing or offline dictionary attacks if hashes are exposed.

**Fix:**
Enforce an adequate minimum password length (e.g. 12 characters) and reasonable upper bound (e.g. 128 characters) during registration.
```java
                if (username == null || username.trim().isEmpty()) {
                    auditLogger.logInvalidInput(correlationId, username, clientIp, "Username cannot be empty during registration", maxFailedAttempts);
                    return false;
                }
                if (password == null || password.length < 12 || password.length > 128) {
                    auditLogger.logInvalidInput(correlationId, username, clientIp, "Password must be between 12 and 128 characters in length", maxFailedAttempts);
                    return false;
                }
```

---

### SEC-07: Exposure of Mutable Internal Byte Arrays for Password Hash and Salt
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-375: Returning a Mutable Object to an Untrusted Caller
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:92-93`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:92-93
        public byte[] getPasswordHash() { return passwordHash; }
        public byte[] getSalt() { return salt; }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
In Java, arrays are mutable objects. `UserAccount.getPasswordHash()` and `UserAccount.getSalt()` return direct references to internal `byte[]` fields. Any external component or caller that obtains a `UserAccount` reference can directly modify the contents of the array (for example, zeroing or modifying elements via `user.getPasswordHash()[0] = 0`), corrupting the stored credentials in memory and causing authentication failures.

**Fix:**
Return defensive copies of internal arrays in getters to maintain encapsulation (CWE-495 / CWE-375).
```java
        public byte[] getPasswordHash() { return passwordHash != null ? passwordHash.clone() : null; }
        public byte[] getSalt() { return salt != null ? salt.clone() : null; }
```

---

### SEC-08: Retention of Plaintext Passwords in Heap Memory via String API and Uncleared `PBEKeySpec`
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-316: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information in Memory
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:194-201`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:194-201
        public static byte[] hashPassword(char[] password, byte[] salt, int iterations) {
            try {
                PBEKeySpec spec = new PBEKeySpec(password, salt, iterations, HASH_LENGTH_BITS);
                SecretKeyFactory factory = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance(HASH_ALGORITHM);
                return factory.generateSecret(spec).getEncoded();
            } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException | InvalidKeySpecException e) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Cryptographic key derivation failed for " + HASH_ALGORITHM, e);
            }
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
1. `PBEKeySpec` creates an internal copy of the `char[] password` array in its constructor. Without explicitly calling `spec.clearPassword()` in a `finally` block, this copy remains in JVM heap memory until the object is garbage-collected.
2. In addition, `AuthenticationService` provides convenience methods (lines 723-733) that accept passwords as immutable `java.lang.String` objects (`authenticate(String username, String password, String clientIp)`). Strings cannot be zeroed out in memory, persisting in the JVM heap and heap dumps.

**Fix:**
Ensure `spec.clearPassword()` is always called in a `finally` block inside `hashPassword()`, and deprecate or remove the `String`-accepting `authenticate()` overloads in favor of `char[]`.
```java
        public static byte[] hashPassword(char[] password, byte[] salt, int iterations) {
            PBEKeySpec spec = null;
            try {
                spec = new PBEKeySpec(password, salt, iterations, HASH_LENGTH_BITS);
                SecretKeyFactory factory = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance(HASH_ALGORITHM);
                return factory.generateSecret(spec).getEncoded();
            } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException | InvalidKeySpecException e) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Cryptographic key derivation failed for " + HASH_ALGORITHM, e);
            } finally {
                if (spec != null) {
                    spec.clearPassword();
                }
            }
        }
```

---

### SEC-09: Locale-Dependent Case Mapping in Username Normalization
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-178: Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity
- **Location:** `AuthenticationSystem.java:152`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthenticationSystem.java:152
            return Optional.ofNullable(users.get(username.toLowerCase().trim()));
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`InMemoryUserRepository` normalizes usernames using `username.toLowerCase().trim()`. In Java, `String.toLowerCase()` without parameters uses the host system's default locale (`Locale.getDefault()`).

In locales such as Turkish (`tr`) or Azeri (`az`), uppercase `'I'` does not convert to lowercase `'i'`; instead it converts to `'\u0131'` (dotless lowercase i), and lowercase `'i'` converts to `'\u0130'` (dotted uppercase I). If the application executes in such a locale, lookups for usernames containing `'I'` or `'i'` (e.g. `"ADMIN"`, `"alice"`) will fail to match or can result in account collision and authorization bypasses.

**Fix:**
Specify `Locale.ROOT` in all `toLowerCase()` operations to ensure deterministic, locale-invariant ASCII case folding.
```java
            return Optional.ofNullable(users.get(username.toLowerCase(java.util.Locale.ROOT).trim()));
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding
- **Cryptographic Password Hashing Algorithm**: Verified in `AuthenticationSystem.PasswordSecurity` (lines 172-202) that passwords are hashed using `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` with 100,000 iterations and a 16-byte random salt generated via `SecureRandom`. Weak algorithms such as MD5, SHA-1, single-iteration SHA-256, and unsalted hashes were verified to be absent.
- **Constant-Time Hash Comparison**: Verified in `AuthenticationSystem.PasswordSecurity.verifyPassword` (line 211) that hash comparisons use `MessageDigest.isEqual()`, mitigating side-channel timing discrepancy attacks on stored password hashes (CWE-208).
- **Non-Existent User Timing Defense**: Verified in `AuthenticationSystem.AuthenticationService.authenticate` (lines 662-666) and `PasswordSecurity.performDummyVerification` (lines 218-223) that authentication requests for non-existent users trigger a full 100,000-iteration PBKDF2 dummy calculation, ensuring response latency is consistent with existing user verifications (CWE-208).
- **Credential Sanitization in Logs**: Verified in `AuthenticationSystem.AuditEvent` (lines 263-314) that neither plaintext passwords, password hashes, nor salts are stored in `AuditEvent` fields or output by `toStructuredLogString()`, preventing credential leakage in log files (CWE-532).
- **Cryptographic Identifier Generation**: Verified in `AuthenticationSystem.AuthenticationService.authenticate` (line 638) that request correlation IDs are generated using `UUID.randomUUID()`, providing cryptographically secure pseudo-random 128-bit identifiers.
- **Immediate Memory Clearing on Normal Paths**: Verified in `AuthenticationSystem.AuthenticationService.authenticate` (line 716) and `registerUser` (line 629) that the submitted `char[] password` is cleared using `Arrays.fill(password, '\0')` in `finally` blocks upon completion.
- **SQL / Command Injection**: Verified that the codebase does not construct SQL queries, LDAP queries, or operating system commands, eliminating CWE-89, CWE-90, and CWE-78 risks.

### 19) results-cyber/agy/agy/set_a/sallie/1/basic/security_review.md

# Security Review: Java Authentication and Session Cookie Application

## 1. Executive Summary
This document provides a static application security review of the standalone Java Authentication and Session Cookie Application located in `/data/results/agy/set_a/sallie/1/basic/`. The application provides an embedded HTTP server (`com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer`) handling user authentication, session token generation, session lifecycle tracking, and HTML/JSON response rendering. Credential verification utilizes salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password hashing with constant-time comparison.

While the core cryptographic verification logic and session token generation mechanisms are implemented securely, the review identified several critical- and high-severity security weaknesses:
1. **Plaintext Secret & Token Logging (High):** Active bearer session tokens are emitted into standard application logs upon login, and demo user passwords are logged during startup.
2. **Hardcoded Credentials & Sensitive Data Exposure (High):** Demo credentials—including the administrator password—are hardcoded and rendered publicly in plaintext on the unauthenticated login web page.
3. **Insecure Session Cookie Transmission (High):** Session cookies omit the `Secure` flag and are served over unencrypted HTTP, allowing session token theft via network eavesdropping.
4. **Denial of Service via Unbounded Request Ingestion (Medium):** Incoming HTTP request bodies are read into memory without size limits, enabling memory exhaustion (`OutOfMemoryError`).
5. **Missing Defensive Security Headers (Medium):** HTTP responses lack standard protective headers (`Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Frame-Options`, `X-Content-Type-Options`), leaving clients exposed to clickjacking and MIME sniffing.

Remediation requires removing secrets from logs and views, enforcing the `Secure` attribute over TLS/HTTPS, bounding request streaming sizes, and configuring standard browser protection headers.

## 2. Scope
| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `AuthApplication.java` | Core application source containing embedded HTTP server, routing, handlers, user database, PBKDF2 hashing, session management, and view templates | Authentication handling, password hashing and verification, session token generation, cookie creation and parsing, request body reading, HTML/JSON rendering, security logging |
| `pom.xml` | Apache Maven project configuration file | Build specifications, Java compiler version (Java 17), dependency definitions (zero external dependencies), packaging configuration |
| `test_app.sh` | Bash integration test script | Starts application, executes automated HTTP test requests using `curl`, verifies cookie issuance, protected endpoints, and session termination |
| `README.md` | Plain-English documentation | Describes system architecture, security features, setup instructions, credentials, and test workflows |

## 3. Skills Applied
- `testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`: Applied to password authentication routines, session lifecycle management, token revocation on logout, and brute-force vulnerability analysis.
- `testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure`: Applied to credential exposure on login pages, secret leakage in application logs, plaintext session cookies, and in-memory credential retention.
- `performing-security-headers-audit`: Applied to HTTP response headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, HSTS) and session cookie attributes (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, `Secure`).
- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: Applied to PBKDF2 parameters (iterations, salt length, key derivation function), PRNG entropy generation (`SecureRandom`), and timing attack resistance (`MessageDigest.isEqual`).
- `testing-for-xss-vulnerabilities`: Applied to view rendering templates, input reflection, and HTML entity encoding routines.
- General OWASP Top 10 / CWE Knowledge:
  - CWE-400 / CWE-770 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption / DoS via unbounded stream reading) was evaluated against general OWASP A04:2021 (Insecure Design) as no specialized library skill addressed JVM stream reading constraints.
  - CWE-290 (Client IP Spoofing via unvalidated `X-Forwarded-For` header) was evaluated against general security engineering practices.
  - CWE-377 (Insecure Temporary File in integration scripts) was evaluated against general operating system security best practices.

## 4. Summary of Findings
| ID | Title | Severity | CWE | Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-01 | Active Session Identifier Logged to Application Logs | High | CWE-532 | `AuthApplication.java:216-217` |
| SEC-02 | Hardcoded User Passwords Displayed on Public Login Page | High | CWE-798 | `AuthApplication.java:926-934` |
| SEC-03 | User Passwords Written to Application Logs at Startup | High | CWE-532 | `AuthApplication.java:90-93` |
| SEC-04 | Missing `Secure` Attribute on Session Cookie Over Plaintext Transport | High | CWE-614 | `AuthApplication.java:410-413` |
| SEC-05 | Unbounded Request Body Ingestion Leading to Denial of Service | Medium | CWE-400 | `AuthApplication.java:428-437` |
| SEC-06 | Missing Defensive HTTP Security Headers | Medium | CWE-693 | `AuthApplication.java:501-504` |
| SEC-07 | Client IP Spoofing via Unvalidated `X-Forwarded-For` Header | Medium | CWE-290 | `AuthApplication.java:420-426` |
| SEC-08 | Absence of Authentication Rate Limiting on Login Endpoints | Low | CWE-307 | `AuthApplication.java:209-211` |
| SEC-09 | Insecure Fixed Temporary File in Test Script | Low | CWE-377 | `test_app.sh:6-8` |

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Active Session Identifier Logged to Application Logs
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:216-217`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:216-217
                LOGGER.info(String.format("[AUTH SUCCESS] User '%s' authenticated. Session ID: %s",
                        username, newSession.getId()));
```

**Why it is a problem:**
When a user logs in successfully, `LoginHandler` writes the newly generated session token (`newSession.getId()`) directly into the application's standard logger output. In production and container environments, log streams are routinely captured by log forwarders, persistent log files, and monitoring dashboards (e.g., CloudWatch, Datadog, ELK). Because session tokens are bearer credentials, anyone with read access to the application logs can extract the active session ID and impersonate the user on `/dashboard` or `/api/session` without providing a password.

**Fix:**
Remove the full session token from the log message. If correlating log entries to session events is required, log only a non-reversible cryptographic hash (e.g. SHA-256 digest) or an internal audit sequence number.
```java
// AuthApplication.java:216-217
                LOGGER.info(String.format("[AUTH SUCCESS] User '%s' authenticated successfully",
                        username));
```

---

### SEC-02: Hardcoded User Passwords Displayed on Public Login Page
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:926-934`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:926-934
            for (User u : demoUsers) {
                sb.append("          <tr>\n");
                sb.append("            <td><code>").append(SecurityUtils.escapeHtml(u.getUsername())).append("</code></td>\n");
                sb.append("            <td><code>").append(SecurityUtils.escapeHtml(u.getDemoPassword())).append("</code></td>\n");
                sb.append("            <td><span class=\"badge ")
                        .append("Administrator".equals(u.getRole()) ? "badge-admin" : "badge-user")
                        .append("\">").append(SecurityUtils.escapeHtml(u.getRole())).append("</span></td>\n");
                sb.append("          </tr>\n");
            }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The HTML login view generated by `Views.renderLoginPage` contains a "Preconfigured Test Accounts" table that displays the usernames and plaintext passwords for all initialized accounts, including the administrator account (`admin` / `AdminPassword123!`). Because `/login` is accessible without authentication, any remote client or automated scanner can read the administrator credentials directly from the page and log in with full privileges. Furthermore, storing the plaintext password in `User.demoPassword` causes cleartext secrets to reside permanently in JVM heap memory.

**Fix:**
Eliminate plaintext password rendering from the login page, remove `demoPassword` from the `User` model, and initialize credentials from secure external configurations or administrative provisioning workflows.
```java
// AuthApplication.java:926-934
            // Remove the table and do not display user credentials on the login page
```

---

### SEC-03: User Passwords Written to Application Logs at Startup
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:90-93`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:90-93
        for (User user : userManager.getAllUsers()) {
            LOGGER.info(String.format("   - Username: %-10s | Password: %-16s | Role: %s",
                    user.getUsername(), user.getDemoPassword(), user.getRole()));
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
During server startup in `AuthApplication.start()`, the application iterates through all registered users and prints their plaintext passwords to console logs. This causes user authentication secrets to be written to console logs, service stdout files, and systemd journals, completely undermining the confidentiality afforded by the PBKDF2 password hashing mechanism.

**Fix:**
Remove the plaintext password output from startup logging statements. Log only non-sensitive account metadata such as usernames and roles.
```java
// AuthApplication.java:90-93
        for (User user : userManager.getAllUsers()) {
            LOGGER.info(String.format("   - Username: %-10s | Role: %s",
                    user.getUsername(), user.getRole()));
        }
```

---

### SEC-04: Missing `Secure` Attribute on Session Cookie Over Plaintext Transport
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:410-413`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:410-413
    public static String buildSetCookieHeader(String sessionId, int maxAgeSeconds) {
        return String.format("%s=%s; Path=/; Max-Age=%d; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict",
                COOKIE_NAME, sessionId, maxAgeSeconds);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
While `buildSetCookieHeader` correctly specifies `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Strict`, it omits the `Secure` flag. Concurrently, the application runs on plain HTTP (`HttpServer.create(...)`). Without the `Secure` attribute, browsers will transmit the `SESSIONID` cookie over unencrypted HTTP connections. An adversary positioned on the local network (e.g., shared Wi-Fi, DNS/ARP spoofing) can capture the session cookie in transit via an Adversary-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack and hijack the authenticated session.

**Fix:**
Append the `Secure` flag to the cookie header and deploy the application using TLS/HTTPS (e.g. `HttpsServer` with an SSLContext, or behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS).
```java
// AuthApplication.java:410-413
    public static String buildSetCookieHeader(String sessionId, int maxAgeSeconds) {
        return String.format("%s=%s; Path=/; Max-Age=%d; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Secure",
                COOKIE_NAME, sessionId, maxAgeSeconds);
    }
```

---

### SEC-05: Unbounded Request Body Ingestion Leading to Denial of Service
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:428-437`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:428-437
    private static String readRequestBody(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        InputStream is = exchange.getRequestBody();
        ByteArrayOutputStream baos = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];
        int bytesRead;
        while ((bytesRead = is.read(buffer)) != -1) {
            baos.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
        }
        return baos.toString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The `readRequestBody` method reads the entire request body from `exchange.getRequestBody()` into a `ByteArrayOutputStream` until the stream terminates, without checking `Content-Length` or imposing an upper bound on bytes read. An unauthenticated attacker can send an arbitrarily large HTTP POST payload (hundreds of megabytes or gigabytes) to `/login` or `/api/login`. Because this data accumulates in the JVM heap, it can rapidly cause a `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError` (OOM), crashing the process and causing a Denial of Service for all users.

**Fix:**
Enforce an explicit byte limit (e.g., 8 KB for authentication forms). If incoming request data exceeds this threshold, abort processing and return HTTP status 413 (Payload Too Large).
```java
// AuthApplication.java:428-437
    private static final int MAX_BODY_BYTES = 8192; // 8 KB limit

    private static String readRequestBody(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        InputStream is = exchange.getRequestBody();
        ByteArrayOutputStream baos = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];
        int bytesRead;
        int totalBytes = 0;
        while ((bytesRead = is.read(buffer)) != -1) {
            totalBytes += bytesRead;
            if (totalBytes > MAX_BODY_BYTES) {
                throw new IOException("Request body exceeds maximum allowed size (" + MAX_BODY_BYTES + " bytes)");
            }
            baos.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
        }
        return baos.toString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }
```

---

### SEC-06: Missing Defensive HTTP Security Headers
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:501-504`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:501-504
    private static void sendHtmlResponse(HttpExchange exchange, int statusCode, String html) throws IOException {
        byte[] bytes = html.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=UTF-8");
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Cache-Control", "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate");
```

**Why it is a problem:**
HTTP responses from `sendHtmlResponse` only include `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control`. They omit essential security headers:
- `X-Frame-Options` and `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`: Leaves the application vulnerable to clickjacking attacks (CWE-1021) by allowing malicious third-party websites to embed the login and dashboard pages inside an `<iframe>`.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`: Leaves browsers open to MIME type sniffing.
- `Content-Security-Policy`: Missing browser-enforced resource and execution boundaries.
- `Referrer-Policy`: Missing explicit control over referrer information leakage.

**Fix:**
Include standard defensive security headers in all HTTP responses.
```java
// AuthApplication.java:501-504
    private static void sendHtmlResponse(HttpExchange exchange, int statusCode, String html) throws IOException {
        byte[] bytes = html.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=UTF-8");
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Cache-Control", "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate");
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Security-Policy", "default-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'");
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin");
```

---

### SEC-07: Client IP Spoofing via Unvalidated `X-Forwarded-For` Header
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-290: Authentication Bypass by Spoofing
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:420-426`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:420-426
    private static String getClientIp(HttpExchange exchange) {
        String xForwardedFor = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Forwarded-For");
        if (xForwardedFor != null && !xForwardedFor.trim().isEmpty()) {
            return xForwardedFor.split(",")[0].trim();
        }
        return exchange.getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress();
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`getClientIp` blindly trusts the client-controlled `X-Forwarded-For` HTTP header without verifying that the request originated from a trusted internal reverse proxy. Any client can supply an arbitrary header value (e.g. `X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1` or `X-Forwarded-For: 192.168.1.100`). This spoofed value is recorded in security audit logs (`[LOGIN ATTEMPT] Username='...' from IP=...`), saved into the `Session` object, and displayed on `/dashboard`, falsifying forensic audit trails and subverting any downstream IP-based controls.

**Fix:**
Use the remote socket address directly unless the incoming connection is verified to originate from a designated, trusted reverse proxy CIDR block.
```java
// AuthApplication.java:420-426
    private static String getClientIp(HttpExchange exchange) {
        // Direct socket address cannot be spoofed by HTTP request headers
        return exchange.getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress();
    }
```

---

### SEC-08: Absence of Authentication Rate Limiting on Login Endpoints
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
- **Location:** `AuthApplication.java:209-211`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// AuthApplication.java:209-211
            LOGGER.info(String.format("[LOGIN ATTEMPT] Username='%s' from IP=%s", username, clientIp));

            Optional<User> user = userManager.authenticate(username, password);
```

**Why it is a problem:**
Neither `/login` nor `/api/login` enforces request rate limiting, failed attempt throttling, or temporary account lockouts. Although PBKDF2 hashing adds computational cost and dummy hashing protects against username enumeration timing differences, attackers can submit rapid, automated brute-force or credential stuffing requests without being throttled or blocked.

**Fix:**
Implement rate limiting or tracking of consecutive failed login attempts keyed by IP address or username, rejecting excessive requests with HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests).
```java
// AuthApplication.java:209-211
            if (isRateLimited(clientIp, username)) {
                sendRedirect(exchange, "/login?error=too_many_attempts");
                return;
            }

            Optional<User> user = userManager.authenticate(username, password);
            if (user.isEmpty()) {
                recordFailedAttempt(clientIp, username);
            } else {
                clearFailedAttempts(clientIp, username);
            }
```

---

### SEC-09: Insecure Fixed Temporary File in Test Script
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-377: Insecure Temporary File
- **Location:** `test_app.sh:6-8`

**Vulnerable code:**
```bash
# test_app.sh:6-8
COOKIE_JAR="/tmp/test_cookies.txt"

rm -f "${COOKIE_JAR}"
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The automated test script stores authentication cookies containing valid session tokens in `/tmp/test_cookies.txt`. Because `/tmp` is shared among all local users on standard Linux systems and the file path is fixed and predictable, an unprivileged local user could observe or pre-create this file (symlink attack) or read the session cookies during automated test execution.

**Fix:**
Create uniquely named temporary files using `mktemp` with restricted permissions (0600).
```bash
# test_app.sh:6-8
COOKIE_JAR=$(mktemp /tmp/test_cookies.XXXXXX)
chmod 600 "${COOKIE_JAR}"
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding
- **Password Hashing Implementation (PBKDF2)**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:768-793`. The application uses standard `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` with 65,536 iterations, 128-bit cryptographically secure random salts per user, and 256-bit derived key length. No deprecated or weak algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256) are used for password storage.
- **Timing Side-Channel Protections**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:682-685` and `AuthApplication.java:794-798`. Hash verification uses `MessageDigest.isEqual` for constant-time byte comparison, avoiding early termination timing attacks. Additionally, when an unrecognized username is submitted, `UserManager.authenticate` calculates a dummy hash with `SecurityUtils.DUMMY_SALT` to ensure uniform response latency and prevent username enumeration.
- **Session Identifier Entropy**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:716` and `AuthApplication.java:800-804`. Session tokens are 32 bytes (256 bits) of cryptographic randomness generated via `java.security.SecureRandom`, converted to 64 hexadecimal characters. Tokens are unpredictable and resilient against offline brute force or guessing.
- **Session Lifecycle & Invalidation**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:639-644`, `AuthApplication.java:703-713`, `AuthApplication.java:730-733`, and `AuthApplication.java:739-743`. Sessions enforce both a 30-minute idle sliding window and a 12-hour absolute lifetime. Expired sessions are removed on access and periodically purged every 60 seconds by a background daemon thread. Both web (`/logout`) and API (`/api/logout`) endpoints immediately invalidate the session server-side and instruct the browser to discard the cookie via `Max-Age=0`.
- **Session Fixation Defense**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:215` and `AuthApplication.java:312`. Upon successful authentication, a brand-new session token is generated via `sessionManager.createSession(...)`, ensuring no pre-authentication session identifier is adopted or reused.
- **CSRF Defense via Cookie Directive**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:411`. The session cookie specifies `SameSite=Strict`, instructing modern user agents not to attach the cookie to cross-origin HTTP requests.
- **Client-Side Script Inaccessibility**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:411`. The `HttpOnly` flag is set on the session cookie, preventing client-side JavaScript (`document.cookie`) from accessing the session token in the event of an XSS vulnerability.
- **HTML Output Encoding**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:814-821` and `AuthApplication.java:946-995`. User-controlled fields (`username`, `fullName`, `role`, `clientIp`, `sessionId`) are sanitized using `SecurityUtils.escapeHtml()` (encoding `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, and `'`) before insertion into HTML views.
- **JSON Serialization Safety**: Verified in `AuthApplication.java:542-551` and `AuthApplication.java:348-352`. Output strings rendered in JSON responses are escaped using `escapeJson()` to prevent JSON injection or format breakage.

### 20) results-cyber/agy/agy/set_a/sallie/1/security/security_review.md

# Security Review: LoginServer (Java Authentication & Session Management Server)

## 1. Executive Summary
The reviewed codebase comprises `LoginServer.java`, a standalone Java HTTP web application implementing user authentication, PBKDF2 password hashing, secure session management with `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Strict` cookies, brute-force rate limiting, and an interactive dashboard demonstrating client-side cookie access controls. While the application implements several robust defense-in-depth controls (such as `SecureRandom` session token generation, constant-time hash comparisons, and strict session expiration), multiple security vulnerabilities were identified. The most significant issues include hardcoded credentials in source code (CWE-798), sensitive cookies issued without the `Secure` attribute by default (CWE-614), DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting via `document.cookie` written into `innerHTML` (CWE-79), missing CSRF validation and GET method acceptance on the logout endpoint (CWE-352), empty-token bypass in login CSRF validation (CWE-352), exposure of credentials in standard output logs (CWE-532), context-mismatched output encoding inside JavaScript blocks (CWE-116), an overly permissive Content Security Policy using `'unsafe-inline'` (CWE-1021), IP-only rate limiting susceptible to distributed brute force (CWE-307), and missing HTTP Strict Transport Security (CWE-319).

## 2. Scope
| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `LoginServer.java` | Standalone HTTP web server implementing user authentication, session lifecycle management, and a security demonstration dashboard | Password hashing and verification using PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256; session generation, expiration, and invalidation; cookie attribute configuration (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, `Secure`); anti-CSRF token handling and double-submit validation; IP-based rate limiting on authentication; HTTP defense headers and CSP generation; HTML/JSON response generation and client-side JavaScript DOM rendering |

## 3. Skills Applied
- `testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`: Applied to assess credential verification mechanisms, session token entropy, session expiration and invalidation logic, and authentication brute-force protections.
- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: Applied to audit PBKDF2 hashing parameters, salt generation, constant-time comparison routines, random number generators, and detect hardcoded secrets.
- `performing-csrf-attack-simulation`: Applied to audit anti-CSRF token generation, double-submit cookie validation, request method restrictions, and logout state-change protections.
- `performing-security-headers-audit`: Applied to evaluate HTTP security response headers (`Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Frame-Options`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Cache-Control`, `Strict-Transport-Security`) and cookie security flags (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, `Secure`).
- `testing-for-xss-vulnerabilities`: Applied to inspect server-side HTML/JSON output escaping and client-side DOM sinks (`innerHTML`) consuming client sources (`document.cookie`).
- General OWASP Top 10 / CWE knowledge: Applied to review credential logging in console output (CWE-532), account-level lockout vs. IP-only throttling (CWE-307), and transport layer security enforcement (CWE-319 / CWE-523).

## 4. Summary of Findings
| ID | Title | Severity | CWE | Location |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-01 | Hardcoded Default and Plaintext User Credentials in Source Code | High | CWE-798 | `LoginServer.java:87-93` |
| SEC-02 | Sensitive Session and CSRF Cookies Issued Without Secure Flag by Default | High | CWE-614 | `LoginServer.java:84` |
| SEC-03 | DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (DOM XSS) via `document.cookie` in Dashboard Script | High | CWE-79 | `LoginServer.java:386-390` |
| SEC-04 | Missing CSRF Protection and Insecure GET Method Acceptance on Logout | Medium | CWE-352 | `LoginServer.java:178-184` |
| SEC-05 | Login Anti-CSRF Validation Accepts Empty Form and Cookie Tokens | Medium | CWE-352 | `LoginServer.java:224-231` |
| SEC-06 | Sensitive Authentication Credentials Exposed in Console Logs | Medium | CWE-532 | `LoginServer.java:124-126` |
| SEC-07 | Context-Mismatched HTML Encoding Inside JavaScript String Literal | Medium | CWE-116 | `LoginServer.java:405-406` |
| SEC-08 | Overly Permissive Content Security Policy with `'unsafe-inline'` Directive | Medium | CWE-1021 | `LoginServer.java:675` |
| SEC-09 | Authentication Rate Limiting Restricted to IP Address Without Account-Level Throttling | Medium | CWE-307 | `LoginServer.java:234-239` |
| SEC-10 | Missing HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Header | Low | CWE-319 | `LoginServer.java:666-680` |

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Hardcoded Default and Plaintext User Credentials in Source Code
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:87-93`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:87-93
        String demoUser = getEnv("DEMO_USERNAME", "admin");
        String demoPass = getEnv("DEMO_PASSWORD", "AdminPassword123!");

        UserStore userStore = new UserStore();
        userStore.addUser(demoUser, demoPass.toCharArray());
        userStore.addUser("alice", "Password123!".toCharArray());
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The application hardcodes a plaintext password (`"Password123!"`) for user `"alice"` directly into the source code, as well as a default fallback password (`"AdminPassword123!"`) for the `"admin"` account when environment variables are not set. Anyone with access to the source code repository, build artifacts, or decompiled bytecode can extract these credentials and gain unauthorized access to the application.

**Fix:**
Remove hardcoded credentials from the source code. Require credentials to be supplied at runtime via environment variables or an external secrets vault, and fail securely if required credentials are not configured.
```java
        String demoUser = getEnv("DEMO_USERNAME", null);
        String demoPass = getEnv("DEMO_PASSWORD", null);

        UserStore userStore = new UserStore();
        if (demoUser != null && demoPass != null && !demoPass.isBlank()) {
            userStore.addUser(demoUser, demoPass.toCharArray());
        }
```

---

### SEC-02: Sensitive Session and CSRF Cookies Issued Without Secure Flag by Default
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:84`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:84
        boolean secureCookie = !"false".equalsIgnoreCase(getEnv("COOKIE_SECURE", "false"));
```

**Why it is a problem:**
`COOKIE_SECURE` defaults to `"false"`. Consequently, both the session cookie (`SESSIONID`) and the login anti-CSRF cookie (`CSRF_TOKEN`) are issued without the `Secure` flag by default. When the `Secure` attribute is omitted, browsers will transmit session identifiers over unencrypted HTTP connections, allowing adversaries on the same local network or in an active man-in-the-middle (MitM) position to intercept and hijack authenticated user sessions.

**Fix:**
Enforce the `Secure` attribute by default so cookies are restricted to encrypted HTTPS channels unless explicitly disabled for isolated local testing.
```java
        boolean secureCookie = !"false".equalsIgnoreCase(getEnv("COOKIE_SECURE", "true"));
```

---

### SEC-03: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (DOM XSS) via `document.cookie` in Dashboard Script
- **Severity:** High
- **CWE:** CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:386-390`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:386-390
                    var cookies = document.cookie;
                    box.style.display = 'block';
                    if (cookies.indexOf('SESSIONID') !== -1) {
                        box.className = 'test-result alert-danger';
                        box.innerHTML = '<strong>Vulnerability!</strong> The SESSIONID cookie was read by JavaScript: ' + cookies;
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The `testReadCookie()` function reads `document.cookie` and concatenates it directly into `box.innerHTML` without sanitization or HTML entity escaping. If any non-HttpOnly cookie accessible in the browser context contains HTML markup or malicious script payloads (e.g. from an attacker via cookie injection, subdomain takeover, or cross-site scripting on a related domain), clicking the button will execute arbitrary JavaScript within the authenticated victim's session.

**Fix:**
Use safe DOM manipulation methods such as `textContent` or `innerText` to display raw cookie strings instead of interpolating them directly into `innerHTML`.
```java
                    var cookies = document.cookie;
                    box.style.display = 'block';
                    if (cookies.indexOf('SESSIONID') !== -1) {
                        box.className = 'test-result alert-danger';
                        box.textContent = 'Vulnerability! The SESSIONID cookie was read by JavaScript: ' + cookies;
```

### SEC-04: Missing CSRF Protection and Insecure GET Method Acceptance on Logout
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:178-184`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:178-184
                case "/logout" -> {
                    if ("POST".equals(method) || "GET".equals(method)) {
                        handleLogout(exchange);
                    } else {
                        sendError(exchange, 405, "Method Not Allowed");
                    }
                }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The `/logout` endpoint accepts both `GET` and `POST` requests and immediately invalidates the server session without validating any anti-CSRF token. While the dashboard rendering includes a hidden `csrf` field, `handleLogout` never inspects or verifies this token. Accepting state-changing `GET` requests allows attackers to perform Logout CSRF by embedding `<img src="http://target:8080/logout">` or sending external links, terminating active user sessions without their knowledge or consent.

**Fix:**
Require the `POST` HTTP method for `/logout`, parse the request payload, and validate the submitted CSRF token against the active session's CSRF token before performing session invalidation.
```java
                case "/logout" -> {
                    requireMethod(method, "POST");
                    handleLogout(exchange);
                }
```
and update `handleLogout` to validate the CSRF token:
```java
    private void handleLogout(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException, HttpException {
        Optional<Session> sessionOpt = resolveCurrentSession(exchange);
        if (sessionOpt.isPresent()) {
            Session session = sessionOpt.get();
            Map<String, String> formData = parseFormData(exchange);
            String submittedCsrf = formData.get("csrf");
            if (submittedCsrf == null || !MessageDigest.isEqual(
                    session.csrfToken().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                    submittedCsrf.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
                throw new HttpException(403, "Invalid CSRF token for logout.");
            }
            sessionStore.invalidate(session.id());
            System.out.printf("[SECURITY] User '%s' logged out. Session invalidated.%n", sanitizeForLog(session.username()));
        }

        String expiredCookie = buildCookieHeader(
                SESSION_COOKIE_NAME,
                "",
                "/",
                0,
                true,
                "Strict",
                this.secureCookie
        );

        exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Set-Cookie", expiredCookie);
        sendRedirect(exchange, "/login");
    }
```

### SEC-05: Login Anti-CSRF Validation Accepts Empty Form and Cookie Tokens
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:224-231`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:224-231
        String csrfCookie = extractCookie(exchange, CSRF_COOKIE_NAME);
        String submittedCsrf = formData.get("csrf");
        if (csrfCookie == null || submittedCsrf == null || !MessageDigest.isEqual(
                csrfCookie.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                submittedCsrf.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            renderLoginForm(exchange, 403, "Your login session expired or CSRF token is invalid. Please try again.");
            return;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The validation check checks whether `csrfCookie` or `submittedCsrf` is `null`, but fails to verify that the tokens are non-empty. If a client transmits an empty cookie header (`Cookie: CSRF_TOKEN=`) and an empty form field (`csrf=`), `extractCookie` returns `""` and `formData.get("csrf")` returns `""`. Because neither value is `null` and `MessageDigest.isEqual("".getBytes(), "".getBytes())` evaluates to `true`, the anti-CSRF check succeeds with empty strings, bypassing CSRF validation on login.

**Fix:**
Ensure both the cookie token and submitted token are non-blank in addition to the null check and constant-time comparison.
```java
        String csrfCookie = extractCookie(exchange, CSRF_COOKIE_NAME);
        String submittedCsrf = formData.get("csrf");
        if (csrfCookie == null || submittedCsrf == null || csrfCookie.isBlank() || submittedCsrf.isBlank()
                || !MessageDigest.isEqual(
                csrfCookie.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                submittedCsrf.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            renderLoginForm(exchange, 403, "Your login session expired or CSRF token is invalid. Please try again.");
            return;
        }
```

### SEC-06: Sensitive Authentication Credentials Exposed in Console Logs
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:124-126`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:124-126
        System.out.println(" Demo Users:");
        System.out.println("   - Username: " + demoUser + "  |  Password: " + demoPass);
        System.out.println("   - Username: alice  |  Password: Password123!");
```

**Why it is a problem:**
During server startup, plaintext passwords and usernames are written directly to standard output. In containerized or production cloud deployments, standard output is aggregated into centralized log storage (e.g. CloudWatch, Elasticsearch, Datadog) or terminal scrollbacks accessible to developers, operators, and monitoring tools, leading to credential leakage.

**Fix:**
Omit passwords entirely from startup logs and console messages.
```java
        System.out.println(" Demo Users configured.");
        System.out.println("   - Username: " + sanitizeForLog(demoUser));
        System.out.println("   - Username: alice");
```

### SEC-07: Context-Mismatched HTML Encoding Inside JavaScript String Literal
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-116: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:405-406`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:405-406
                        fetch('/api/session').then(function(res) { return res.json(); }).then(function(data) {
                            if (data.authenticated && data.username === '%s') {
```

**Why it is a problem:**
In `handleGetDashboard`, `session.username()` is formatted into a JavaScript single-quoted string literal within a `<script>` tag using `escapeHtml()` (line 429). `escapeHtml()` replaces characters like `'` with HTML numeric entities (`&#39;`). Because browsers do not decode HTML entities inside `<script>` blocks, the JavaScript runtime compares against the literal string `"&#39;"`, causing functional errors. Furthermore, `escapeHtml()` does not escape backslashes (`\`) or line terminators; if a username contains or ends with a backslash, it escapes the enclosing quote and causes JavaScript syntax errors or breaks out of the string literal into the script execution context.

**Fix:**
Use JSON string serialization or dedicated JavaScript string escaping (`escapeJson()`) when interpolating dynamic data into JavaScript string literals, and enclose in double quotes.
```java
                        fetch('/api/session').then(function(res) { return res.json(); }).then(function(data) {
                            if (data.authenticated && data.username === "%s") {
```
and format using `escapeJson`:
```java
                escapeJson(session.username())
```

### SEC-08: Overly Permissive Content Security Policy with `'unsafe-inline'` Directive
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames / CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:675`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:675
        h.set("Content-Security-Policy", "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'");
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The `script-src` directive includes `'unsafe-inline'`, which allows the execution of arbitrary inline scripts and inline DOM event handlers. This largely defeats the primary security defense provided by Content Security Policy against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), as any injected script payload will execute without restriction.

**Fix:**
Eliminate `'unsafe-inline'` from `script-src` by refactoring inline scripts to external JavaScript files or using cryptographic nonces (`'nonce-...'`).
```java
        h.set("Content-Security-Policy", "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self'");
```

---

### SEC-09: Authentication Rate Limiting Restricted to IP Address Without Account-Level Throttling
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:234-239`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:234-239
        String clientIp = getClientIp(exchange);
        if (rateLimiter.isBlocked(clientIp)) {
            exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Retry-After", String.valueOf(RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW.toSeconds()));
            renderLoginForm(exchange, 429, "Too many failed login attempts. Please wait 15 minutes before trying again.");
            return;
        }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
Authentication failures are tracked solely against the client IP address (`clientIp`). An attacker executing a distributed brute-force or credential stuffing attack using rotating proxies, botnets, or mobile IP pools can target a specific account (`admin`) with an unlimited number of login attempts while staying below the 5-attempt threshold per IP. Additionally, a malicious actor can deliberately lock out all legitimate users behind a corporate NAT or shared gateway IP by generating 5 failed attempts from that IP.

**Fix:**
Implement composite rate limiting that tracks and throttles failed authentication attempts by both client IP address and targeted username.
```java
        String clientIp = getClientIp(exchange);
        String username = formData.getOrDefault("username", "").trim().toLowerCase();
        if (rateLimiter.isBlocked(clientIp) || (!username.isEmpty() && rateLimiter.isAccountBlocked(username))) {
            exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Retry-After", String.valueOf(RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW.toSeconds()));
            renderLoginForm(exchange, 429, "Too many failed login attempts. Please wait 15 minutes before trying again.");
            return;
        }
```

### SEC-10: Missing HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Header
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
- **Location:** `LoginServer.java:666-680`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// LoginServer.java:666-680
    private static void setSecurityHeaders(HttpExchange exchange) {
        Headers h = exchange.getResponseHeaders();
        // Prevent browsers from MIME-sniffing response content
        h.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
        // Defend against clickjacking
        h.set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
        // Strict Referrer Policy
        h.set("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin");
        // Content Security Policy
        h.set("Content-Security-Policy", "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'");
        // Prevent caching of sensitive authenticated content
        h.set("Cache-Control", "no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0");
        h.set("Pragma", "no-cache");
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:**
The security headers omit `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS). When running in production over HTTPS, the absence of HSTS allows attackers to perform SSL stripping attacks on initial plaintext HTTP requests, downgrading user connections to unencrypted HTTP.

**Fix:**
Add the `Strict-Transport-Security` header to enforce HTTPS across all browser interactions.
```java
    private static void setSecurityHeaders(HttpExchange exchange) {
        Headers h = exchange.getResponseHeaders();
        // Enforce HTTPS via HSTS
        h.set("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains");
        // Prevent browsers from MIME-sniffing response content
        h.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
        // Defend against clickjacking
        h.set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
        // Strict Referrer Policy
        h.set("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin");
        // Content Security Policy
        h.set("Content-Security-Policy", "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'");
        // Prevent caching of sensitive authenticated content
        h.set("Cache-Control", "no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0");
        h.set("Pragma", "no-cache");
    }
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding
- HttpOnly Cookie Flag Enforcement: Verified in `buildCookieHeader` (`LoginServer.java:277-285, 576-579`). The `HttpOnly` flag is strictly appended to `SESSIONID` cookies, successfully preventing client-side scripts (`document.cookie`) from reading or writing the session cookie.
- SameSite Cookie Attribute: Verified in `buildCookieHeader` (`LoginServer.java:283, 581-583`). Cookies are configured with `SameSite=Strict`, preventing cross-site request forgery via ambient cookie transmission.
- Cryptographically Secure Session ID Generation: Verified in `generateSecureToken` and `createSession` (`LoginServer.java:612-616, 931-938`). Session tokens are generated using `java.security.SecureRandom` with 32 bytes (256 bits) of cryptographic entropy and URL-safe Base64 encoding.
- Session Invalidation on Logout: Verified in `handleLogout` (`LoginServer.java:436-455`). Active sessions are purged from the server-side `SessionStore` and an expired cookie header (`Max-Age=0`) is issued.
- Session Fixation Mitigation: Verified in `handlePostLogin` (`LoginServer.java:265-273`). Pre-existing sessions are invalidated upon successful authentication before issuing a fresh session identifier.
- Server-Enforced Session Timeouts: Verified in `Session.isExpired` and `SessionStore.findSession` (`LoginServer.java:922-925, 948-957`). Enforces both a 30-minute rolling idle timeout and an 8-hour maximum absolute session lifetime.
- Background Expiration Purging: Verified in `cleanupExpiredSessions` and the scheduled executor (`LoginServer.java:104-109, 139-142, 965-968, 1042-1048`). Expired sessions and old rate-limiter timestamps are periodically purged, mitigating memory exhaustion denial of service.
- Password Hashing with PBKDF2: Verified in `UserStore.hashPassword` (`LoginServer.java:1006-1014`). Uses `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` with 100,000 iterations and a unique 16-byte cryptographically random salt per user.
- Constant-Time Comparison for Hashes and Tokens: Verified in `UserStore.verifyPassword` and `handlePostLogin` (`LoginServer.java:226, 1003`). Employs `MessageDigest.isEqual()` to prevent timing side-channel attacks during credential and token comparisons.
- Timing Side-Channel Protection on Non-Existent Users: Verified in `UserStore.verifyPassword` (`LoginServer.java:995-1000`). Performs a dummy PBKDF2 computation when a queried username is not found, preventing user enumeration via timing discrepancies.
- Generic Authentication Failure Messages: Verified in `handlePostLogin` (`LoginServer.java:258`). Responds with "Invalid username or password" regardless of whether the account exists or the password was incorrect, preventing username enumeration.
- Clickjacking Protection: Verified in `setSecurityHeaders` (`LoginServer.java:671`). Sets `X-Frame-Options: DENY` on all responses to prevent UI redressing attacks.
- MIME Sniffing Prevention: Verified in `setSecurityHeaders` (`LoginServer.java:669`). Employs `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` across all responses.
- Browser Cache Prevention for Sensitive Endpoints: Verified in `setSecurityHeaders` (`LoginServer.java:677-678`). Sets `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0` and `Pragma: no-cache` to ensure sensitive authenticated pages are not cached.
- Request Body Size Bounds: Verified in `parseFormData` (`LoginServer.java:636-639`). Enforces an 8 KB maximum request body size (`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_SIZE`), preventing denial-of-service through excessive payload transmission.
- Input Length Bounds Validation: Verified in `handlePostLogin` (`LoginServer.java:244-250`). Validates that input fields do not exceed 256 characters (`MAX_FIELD_LENGTH`).
- Log Injection Sanitization: Verified in `sanitizeForLog` (`LoginServer.java:738-741`). Replaces newline characters (`\r`, `\n`) with underscores to prevent log forging and carriage return injection in server logs.
